strengths: Novel core insight: GHNs with CNN decoders structurally align weight spaces, enabling patch-based width-agnostic generation. Figure 3 provides compelling visual evidence.
Addresses a real limitation of prior methods that couple generation to fixed matrix dimensions, enabling practical benefits for hardware-constrained deployment.
Strong empirical results: >85% success on unseen topologies while baselines degrade to 59-42%, demonstrating genuine generalization rather than memorization.

Comprehensive experimental validation within scope: ablations show alignment without mode collapse (Table 1, 6), clear seen/unseen separation (Table 2), joint generation capability (Table 3), and diversity analysis.
Rigorous evaluation domain: robotic manipulation is a strict metric where small weight errors cause failure, unlike vision tasks; direct deployment in ManiSkill3.
Clear presentation: well-written with intuitive multimodal tokenization scheme (discrete architecture tokens + continuous weight patches), logical flow, and good visualizations.
Solid technical execution: the MoNL framework adaptation for dual-modality generation is well-implemented with appropriate conditioning schemes.
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope undermines generality claims: only 4-layer MLPs tested (acknowledged in Section 7 as computational constraint), only {16, 32, 64} width vocabulary, only 3 simple robotic tasks, no other architecture classes (CNNs, Transformers).

Core contribution rests on empirical observation without theoretical justification: why specifically do CNN decoders induce locality bias? No ablation on decoder architecture (MLP vs Transformer decoders). Mechanism is stated but not rigorously explained.

Circular dependency in dataset construction: training data generated entirely by GHNs (128 GHNs, top-100 per arch), then NNiT learns GHN-conditioned distribution. Model doesn't learn to generate arbitrary MLPs but rather GHN-compatible ones.

Baseline comparisons lack fairness: SANE fails dramatically (1% on training set) but no ablation validates explanation; D2NWG retains 89% on PushCube unseen widths (attributed to task simplicity without deeper investigation); no methods target width-agnostic generation so adapted baselines aren't purpose-built.

Critical technical details underspecified: patch size p never explicitly stated, weight extraction/cropping mechanism for varying widths not detailed, decoder architecture referenced externally, no sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters.

Experimental design issues: top-10 selection from 100 samples introduces selection bias; MoNL 50-50 joint/conditional ratio unjustified with no ablation; small test set (8/72 architectures); comparison to just training small networks directly not provided.
Missing ablation studies: no ablation on patch size p, MoNL ratio, GHN vs alternative hypernetwork designs, or CNN decoder architecture choices—these are essential for validating design decisions.

Insufficient practical utility analysis: generating policies is niche; training time for generative model not reported; inference requires sampling 100 policies; unclear when this beats direct training of small networks.

Theoretical grounding weak: permutation symmetry proof (Eq. 1) is standard; connection between structural alignment and patchification underexplored; why alignment enables patchification deserves formal treatment.
Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned, some hyperparameters scattered across appendix, GHN details referenced externally, patch size p left unspecified in main text.

Compelling empirical demonstration of structural alignment in GHN-generated weights (Figure 3, Table 1) with proper diversity analysis
Strong empirical results on test domain (85-99% success on unseen MLP architectures vs. baseline failures)
Technically sound multimodal framework combining diffusion transformers with architecture generation via MoNL
Comprehensive experimental details including hyperparameters, dataset construction, and qualitative rollouts
Honest discussion of limitations regarding scalability to deeper networks and computational constraints

Weak baseline comparisons: SANE fails completely on training data (1% success; Table 2) suggesting implementation issues or unfair setup; D2NWG not designed for unseen architectures; no comparison to simpler transfer learning baselines or other GHN-based approaches

Missing essential ablations: effect of patch size, decoder architecture, GHN pretraining necessity, MoNL vs. simpler conditioning, and impact of distance from training widths on generalization performance

Unrealistic evaluation protocol: reporting top-10 from 100 samples is impractical; no analysis of sample efficiency or quality distribution; unclear how performance scales with increased width range or depth

Overstated claims: title and abstract claim 'width-agnostic' generation but evaluation demonstrates only modest width variation; missing details on bias/layer-norm handling in patch tokenization

Scalability unresolved: authors acknowledge difficulty training deeper networks (Section 7) with only speculative solutions (borrowing from pixel-space methods); practical limits of the approach remain unclear

Strong empirical validation of core claims with 35-seed experiments showing consistent alignment without mode collapse (Figure 3, Table 1)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with both conditional and joint generation, multiple robotic tasks, and qualitative policy rollouts demonstrating functional correctness
Elegant technical approach using patch-based tokenization that naturally extends ideas from image generation to weight generation
Detailed experimental methodology with reproducible hyperparameters and dataset generation procedures in appendices
Honest discussion of limitations and concrete suggestions for future work (stabilization from pixel diffusion, video diffusion optimizations)

Test set generalization somewhat limited: 8 unseen architectures drawn from same distribution as training set (64 architectures, same width vocabulary); 'zero-shot' term slightly misleading

strengths: Novel contribution addressing genuine limitation: Width-agnostic weight generation overcomes the fixed-dimensional coupling problem of prior vectorization-based methods (SANE, D2NWG)

Strong empirical insight and validation: GHNs with CNN decoders demonstrably induce structural alignment (r≈0.65 cross-seed correlation, Figure 3) without mode collapse (L2 distance 54.66), with permutation ablation proving necessity
Convincing zero-shot transfer results: >85% success on unseen architectures vs. 1-59% for baselines; NNiT's worst-case (64.8%) exceeds D2NWG's mean (15.6%)
Comprehensive experimental suite: Multiple robotic tasks, MNIST validation, extensive ablations including CKA analysis, diversity metrics, and deployment pipeline

Genuine technical innovation: Multimodal joint architecture-weight generation p(a,w) is novel and achieves 99-100% success; patch-based tokenization elegantly decouples generation from fixed dimensions
Methodologically sound: Mixture of Noise Levels adaptation for dual-modality conditioning is clean; experimental design appropriately tests main claims
Honest limitations discussion: Clearly acknowledges 4-layer restriction and proposes stabilization techniques for deeper networks rather than overclaiming scalability
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: Restricted to 4-layer MLPs (acknowledged computational limitation but undermines generality claims); vocabulary only {16,32,64}; only 3 robotic tasks; insufficient to support broad width-agnostic claims

Problematic circular dependency on GHNs: Requires task-specific GHN training first (128 GHNs, 500-1500 iterations); no computational cost comparison to SGD; generalization tested only on ManiSkill3 variants, not truly different domains
Overclaimed width-agnosticism: Model only handles widths within training vocabulary; cannot generate arbitrary widths; padding strategy (H×W grid) limits maximum width; more accurate framing needed

Baseline comparison fairness concerns: SANE's 1% success seems suspiciously poor with limited justification for adaptation fairness; D2NWG designed for fixed architectures; missing comparisons with recent cited generative models (Liang et al. 2024, Saragih et al. 2025)

Insufficient structural alignment explanation: Claim that GHNs 'collapse permutation symmetries' stated but not formally proven; no ablation comparing CNN vs. other decoder architectures; locality bias explanation is intuitive but not theoretically justified

Methodology limitations: Top-10 selection metric (generating 100, selecting 10) is artificial—practical deployment needs high single-sample success rates; suspiciously high joint generation rates (99-100%) raise questions whether model learned training distribution rather than true generation; custom StackCubeEasy-v1 task appears engineered for stability

Reproducibility and practical concerns: No code/data release; training cost not reported; dataset filtering is task-specific; MNIST evaluation downsamples 784→32 via PCA; promised meta-learning and hardware optimization applications mentioned but never demonstrated

Missing technical details and ablations: No study of patch size effects; no analysis of vocabulary size sensitivity; asymmetry between depth and width transfer not discussed; MoNL framework details relegated to appendix; interaction between architecture tokens and weight patches in self-attention unclear

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real challenges in neural network generation (permutation symmetry and architecture coupling)
Strong empirical validation of structural alignment through multiple complementary analyses (visual heatmaps, diversity metrics, permutation ablation, CKA)
Comprehensive experimental documentation and supporting analyses; demonstrates clear performance gains (85-99% success vs. near-zero baseline) on tested setting
Clear presentation with informative figures and extensive appendices
Good ablation on structural alignment dependency (Section C.2 permutation ablation)
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only 4-layer MLPs, width vocabulary {16,32,64}, 3 robotic tasks—fails to convincingly demonstrate 'width-agnostic' generation claims across meaningful scope
Misleading 'width-agnostic' framing: method requires pre-specifying maximum width M; widths larger than training maximum unclear; should be described as 'width-flexible within bounded range'
Fundamental circular dependency inadequately addressed: GHN generation requires explicit architecture specification, but for truly unseen widths the GHN training distribution construction is unclear

Unfair baseline comparisons: SANE tested outside its design assumptions; D2NWG benefits from same GHN pre-alignment; missing comparisons with concurrent methods (Saragih et al. 2025, Li et al. 2025b); no isolated ablation of patch tokenization vs. flattening

Lack of theoretical justification for core claim: why CNN decoders create local correlations is provided only as intuition; whether this is specific to CNN decoders unexplored; mechanism is pure empirical observation

Critical ablations missing: patch size hyperparameter not ablated; GHN decoder architecture choice (CNN vs. alternatives) unjustified; padding scheme appears ad-hoc; limited analysis of when alignment breaks down
Evaluation concerns: success metric is task-dependent and loose; no failure case analysis; no systematic study of generalization vs. width difference magnitude or depth
Dataset construction bias: using curated top-100 policies may not be representative of natural parameter distributions; unclear if properties hold for standard SGD training
Limited conceptual novelty: patch tokenization from prior work (DiT/FiT); GHNs from prior work; main contribution is observing empirical alignment phenomenon and combining existing techniques
Reproducibility issues: code availability not mentioned; heavy ManiSkill3 dependency; hyperparameter choices often unjustified; replicating GHN training pipeline complex

strengths: Addresses genuine and important limitation: existing neural network generation methods fail to generalize across layer widths

Novel and well-validated insight that GHNs with CNN decoders induce structural weight alignment, confirmed through visualization (Figure 3), diversity metrics (Table 1), permutation ablation, and CKA analysis
Strong empirical results: >85% success on unseen topologies vs. 59% (D2NWG) and 1% (SANE), consistent across three robotic tasks with varying precision requirements
Elegant technical approach: patch-based tokenization naturally extends from image generation, multimodal MoNL training elegantly unifies architecture and weight generation in single framework

Comprehensive experimental validation: extensive ablations (alignment necessity via permutation, diversity via nearest neighbor, functional diversity via CKA), full distribution analysis showing NNiT worst-case (64.8%) exceeds D2NWG mean (15.6%)
Joint generation achieves near-perfect success (99-100%) on easier tasks and demonstrates spontaneous architecture-weight synthesis without fixed topology constraints
Generalization to MNIST (96.1% accuracy) suggests alignment property is task-agnostic rather than robotic-control-specific
Well-written with clear presentation of concepts; extensive appendices provide hyperparameters, additional analyses, and visualizations supporting main claims
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only 4-hidden-layer MLPs with widths from {16, 32, 64}; no evaluation on deeper networks, different depth distributions, or widths outside vocabulary; width-agnostic claims overstate actual generalization (really: combinations within fixed vocabulary)

Fundamental dependency on GHN preprocessing: method learns distributions over GHN-generated weights only; cannot generate arbitrary functional networks; creates circularity of using GHNs to align then modeling GHN-aligned weights; computational cost of training 128 GHNs not analyzed; practical utility unclear versus direct GHN use

Baseline concerns: SANE achieves only 1% success on all settings (seen and unseen), suggesting implementation rather than fundamental limitations; only two baselines compared; no comparison to alternative alignment methods; no ablation validating CNN decoder necessity over alternatives

Incomplete mechanism analysis: Section 4 explanation of why CNN decoders induce alignment is superficial; lacks rigorous treatment of why locality bias produces consistent cross-seed alignment; unclear whether spatial structure is necessary (not just helpful) for patch-based generation; alternative alignment approaches not explored

Architecture representation limitations: discrete sequence formulation suitable only for MLPs; cannot handle branching, skip connections, or modern architectures; CNN generalization mentioned in abstract but never demonstrated; claims about unseen architecture generalization actually refer to unseen width combinations

Missing critical ablations: no sensitivity to patch size p, maximum width M, or vocabulary size; no comparison of GHN decoder architectures (CNN vs. MLP); insufficient analysis of MoNL noise scheduling choices

MNIST validation inadequate: relegated to Appendix H; requires significant preprocessing (PCA downsampling to 32D), reducing confidence in task-independence claims; should be in main paper if task-generality claimed

Reproducibility challenges: GHN dependency complicates reproduction; no code availability mentioned; complex dataset construction (filtering top-100 per architecture) lacks justification; unexplained choices (why 128 GHNs? why top-100?)
Statistical rigor: no significance tests reported; some error bars substantial (e.g., D2NWG StackCubeEasy 27.18±2.35); limited discussion of statistical meaningfulness of differences

Incomplete joint generation analysis: only 53/81 unique architectures from 100 samples with no analysis of architectural bias; single architecture diversity analysis (Figure 6) shows one redundancy without deeper investigation
